units.title: Sparks and the First Battery
units.blurb: Franklin's experiments with lightning, and Volta's pile, the first steady current.

units.title: Magnets and Motion
units.blurb: Faraday turns electricity into motion, and motion into electricity.

units.title: Light and Power
units.blurb: Edison's invention factory and light bulb, and Tesla's alternating-current motor.

topics.title: Benjamin Franklin: Lightning, the Rod, the Stove and Bifocals
topics.short: Printer, writer and experimenter (1706–1790) who showed lightning is electricity, invented the lightning rod, and never patented his inventions.
topics.trouble: People picture lightning striking Franklin's kite; his account says only that the string became charged, and a direct strike could have killed him.

topics.title: Alessandro Volta: The Pile of 1800
topics.short: An Italian professor (1745–1827) who stacked zinc, copper and brine-soaked card into the first battery, after a long debate with Galvani about frogs' legs.
topics.trouble: People think Galvani was simply wrong; both men were partly right, since nerves and muscles do use electricity.

topics.title: Michael Faraday: The Motor and the Generator
topics.short: A bookbinder's apprentice (1791–1867) who became the great experimenter of the Royal Institution: the first motor in 1821, induction in 1831.
topics.trouble: People expect a magnet sitting still in a coil to make current; only a changing magnetic field does.

topics.title: Samuel Morse: The Telegraph and Its Code
topics.short: A painter turned inventor (1791–1872) who, with Alfred Vail and Joseph Henry's science, sent messages along a wire in dots and dashes.
topics.trouble: People think Morse invented the electric telegraph alone; Cooke and Wheatstone in Britain had one working too, and Vail did much of the work.

topics.title: Alexander Graham Bell: The Telephone
topics.short: A teacher of deaf students (1847–1922) who turned the shape of a sound wave into a changing current, and patented the telephone in 1876.
topics.trouble: People think only one person could have invented the telephone; Elisha Gray and Antonio Meucci also have claims, and historians still discuss them.

topics.title: Thomas Edison: Menlo Park and the Light Bulb
topics.short: An inventor (1847–1931) who made invention a team job at Menlo Park: the phonograph in 1877, then a long-lasting bulb after testing thousands of materials.
topics.trouble: People say Edison invented the light bulb from nothing; many inventors had made bulbs, and his team made one that lasted and a system to power it.

topics.title: Nikola Tesla: The Rotating Magnetic Field
topics.short: An engineer (1856–1943) who pictured a motor with no brushes, driven by a magnetic field that turns, and made alternating current practical.
topics.trouble: People tell the war of the currents as heroes and villains; it was a business and engineering contest with good arguments on both sides at the time.
